utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-42/2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vladimir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Phillip Weiner for the Office of the Prosecutor. On the left is David Re, and to the right is Gina Butler. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Howard Morrison, lead counsel for the accused, assisted by Tanja Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. We are here this afternoon to discuss or at least to hear from the parties how they think we should proceed in this case after we have received additional information. Before continuing, I would like to go into private session just for a very short moment in order to discuss a practical matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar. Thank you, Ms. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn for 20 minutes, I'd like to explain to the public what the Chamber did over the last one hour and a half. The Chamber has discussed in more detail with the parties the content of psychiatric reports that have been produced in respect of Mr. Kovacevic. The Chamber has asked additional questions to the psychiatrist who works in the UN Detention Unit in order to better understand the testimony, and the Chamber has invited the parties to give its views on some of these medical matters, including treatment that might be needed. We will adjourn until twenty-five minutes past four, and then after we have recommenced, the Chamber would like to finish in approximately half an hour the remaining issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After having discussed quite a lot of details on the medical and psychiatric condition of Mr. Kovacevic, I'd like to move to another subject at this moment. But before we do so, Mr. Kovacevic, I forgot to ask you at the beginning of the hearing if you could hear us in a language that you understand, but since I did not hear any protest from you, I take it that you could hear us. Is that correct? Yes? Could you please speak aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this just be a bit slower, please, a bit slower?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether the translation comes quick to you. I think I'm not speaking that quickly, but you could follow whatever has been said before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you could understand what was being said because it was all about you as you may be aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. The next issue I'd like to raise is the following one: Is there any common understanding between the parties on the test to be applied? What is needed to determine that someone is fit or unfit to stand trial? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution's submission is that the test should be, or based upon our own survey of national jurisdictions indeed as the Trial Chamber put in its order of the 27th of November last year in which it posed a number of questions for the psychiatrists to comment upon in their report. That was Dr. Goreta and Dr. Krajnovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got the report in front of me. We have put seven questions to them, but these are mainly questions in respect of whether or not the accused could perform certain tasks. Is the performance of tasks the test as we find it in many jurisdictions where we have a list, either statutory list or a list created by case law, that if you are able to perform those tasks that you're fit to stand trial, or the other way round, that if you're not able to perform those tasks that you're unfit to stand trial. Whereas in other systems we have other tests like whether you are able to participate in the proceedings or some other test as mainly concentrating on the understanding of the witness rather -- of the accused rather than the performance of tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not wish to make any submissions in relation to having a finalised view as to what the test is. The Prosecutor's view is that this is not a matter which arises just yet but is something that should be revisited, we say, in six months' time when the accused has had more treatment. The Prosecutor, at the moment, has no difficulty with the questions which the Trial Chamber posed to the psychiatrist in terms of evaluating the accused's competency to enter a plea as the -- as a working basis for a working definition in a preliminary sense moving towards possibly an eventual finalisation of her view on what the test is, but our preliminary view is this is a good start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, any observations from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, my first observation is that that's wonderfully Delphic. I look forward to seeing what the Prosecutor's finalisation of her view on what the test is in -- with a moderate amount of excitement. But I take it that the Prosecutor divides the issue into two. First of all a test as to whether or not somebody is fit to enter a plea, and secondly, whether or not they're fit to stand trial. It seems to me that from a practical point of view, at any one time that's a distinction really without a difference, because if you're not fit to enter a plea, then the trial which would inevitably follow from the entering of a plea of not guilty or procedure which would follow from entering a plea of guilty simply doesn't take place, so that the two are so interdependent that from a psychiatric point of view, I can't see the value of trying to draw any distinction. That said, I respectfully agree with the questions that the Trial Chamber posed to the psychiatrists that if answered in the negative, that the accused simply didn't have the mental capacity to answer those questions in a way which would enable the Trial Chamber to say that in their judgement he was fit to enter a plea, that that is a sufficient basis for the Trial Chamber to make its determination. And as I understand it, and I will be corrected, that there is no real dissent certainly between the Prosecution and the defence that as far as those questions are concerned and as far as those answers which have been submitted by the professionals, we are all of one mind, that as matters stand today, the defendant is not fit upon those tests to enter a plea and, therefore, not fit as matters stand today to stand trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Mr. Re, is the conclusion of Mr. Morrison that the Prosecution is inclined to make a distinction between the competence to enter a plea and the competence or the ability to stand trial is -- is that a correct understanding of your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As Mr. Morrison says, it's a distinction without a real difference. In practical terms, it is the same. The Prosecutor's view is that if the accused is unfit to enter a plea, you then move to a proper psychological or psychiatric testing to determine whether or not the accused may become fit to stand trial, that the two overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a temporal matter. So whether his condition will change in such a way that he might be able to -- at a later stage to enter a plea or stand trial. Let me just put the question in another way. Is it the position of the Prosecution that it's imaginable that someone would be fit to enter a plea and at the same time not be fit to stand trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's view is that these matters -- that second matter doesn't arise for determination at the moment because we have a situation where the accused is, on the reports at least, unfit to or unable to enter a plea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor wishes to leave it at that for the moment pending further psychiatric treatment before expressing a view as to the exact overlap between the two if there is in fact a difference in the tests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I have some difficulties in understanding how psychiatric treatment could elucidate the legal issue. I'll leave it to you at least, to give to us a more -- month perhaps to think it over and to see whether there's any distinction between made. Then there is another issue which might be of direct relevance, and that is the issue that if the Chamber would decide that Mr. Kovacevic would be in need of treatment at this moment and not treatment in the UN Detention Unit but in an institution or a facility outside of that Detention Unit, what would be the proper legal basis to organise this treatment? Would it provisional release? Would it be a modification of detention, of the detention as such? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecutor's view is that her primary submission is the Trial Chamber can treat the accused as a person on remand in need of treatment, and the President could make, or could question modification of the conditions of detention pursuant to Rule 64, that is that the accused be detained somewhere in a secure psychiatric institution as a modification of his present detention by the Tribunal. The Prosecutor, of course, also notes Rule 65(C), which is provisional release subject to whatever conditions the Trial Chamber may deem appropriate. The Prosecutor's primary submission is that if the accused is to be detained anywhere other than the UN Detention Unit at Scheveningen, that it be done via Rule 64 modification. The short reasons for this are that the accused did not surrender voluntarily, and in circumstances where another accused in the same case, that is Pavle Strugar was provisionally released, there was, so to speak, a standoff before he was returned to The Hague for trial commencing at the end of last year. The reports which Your Honours have dealt with have indicated a condition of danger, and the Prosecutor's view is that the interests of the community would be better served if it were a modification of detention rather than a provisional release as such. But having said that, the Prosecutor does take a practical view of this and does recognise that both ends of this -- the ends could be achieved by an order either under Rule 64 or 65(C), but the primary preference is 64. Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner reminds me that the Prosecutor would seek, if it were to be provisional release, identical conditions to those which would be a modification to detention under Rule 64, held in a secure psychiatric institution with appropriate treatment as determined by the court-appointed experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Should the accused under those circumstances make himself available for treatment or should he accept treatment or should he cooperate with this treatment? I hope you understand what the formulation of this condition might not be that easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honours excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can Mr. Weiner address you on that exact point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weiner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. There is a great deal of case law out of the United States in relation to forced treatment or forced medication, and if the accused does not agree to treatment or medication based on his situation, it would be our view that he could be forced to be given medication. One, he could be forced to be given medication which would bring him to a position that he would become competent to stand trial. The case -- or the latest case on that out of the United States is Sell, which is S-e-l-l, versus the United States. It's a 2000 -- it's a June 16th 2003 case. There is an earlier case which has a different twist to it which also concerns this defendant which concerns a situation where a person could be forced to be given medication where he is in detention and he is a danger to himself and/or the community. And the leading case on that out of the United States is Washington versus Harper, and the citation for that is 494 US 210, February 27, 1990. By being placed in a facility under either Rule 64 where it's just a modification of his detention or under Rule 65 where -- where he's being provisionally released; however, under certain conditions and requirements. So it's really a modification of his detention, under either one, he should be ordered to undergo treatment. And if at some time he refuses treatment, refuses medication and his condition gets worse, a hearing should be held here ordering forced medication or at least a request would be made for an order of medication if that would bring him to a point where he would no longer be a danger to himself, to others, and he would be competent to stand -- to offer a plea and stand trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any case law from outside the US, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I could get some, but I think it's sad that there seems to be a lot of insanity cases out of the United States, but I could see what we would be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't suggest that it was any bigger problem in the United States than somewhere else, but you'll understand that US case law is first of all to be applied in the US, and of course it could be of some guidance to this Chamber, but the Chamber always prefers to have a broader basis for its decision than law coming from one specific domestic jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will see what we can find very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further comments in this respect? Defence? Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Dealing with the initial distinction between Rule 64 and Rule 65, the Defence would respectfully submit that Rule 65 is in fact a better vehicle for the Trial Chamber for three reasons. First of all, under Rule 64, one would have to find exceptional circumstances. It may well be that that would not pose a great deal of difficulty if one was to say that the psychiatric condition was an exceptional -- was a circumstance which the drafters of the statute meant to be included in the word "exceptional." The second problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's even easier. You only have to look at the draft of the Rules, didn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The second point is that it devolves upon the President himself where it means the President has to be seize much all the facts in the case and is going to involve the determination by a party who presently has no immediate knowledge or control of this case. And thirdly, the problem arises in my view in this way, that the wording of Rule 64 speaks that "the President may on the application of a party request modification." Now, the words "may" and the word "request" do not provide in my submission anything like the certainty of Rule 65(C), which says: "The Trial Chamber may impose such conditions upon the release of the accused ..." This gives direct control of the case to the Trial Chamber, absolves the President from the necessity of being involved, and involves the imposition of conditions rather than the requesting of conditions. It seems to us on the Defence side that there being no real distinction between the imperative nature of a change of detention or change of remand and a provisional release with imposed conditions that the additional flexibility of Rule 65 is the more attractive option. And as the -- of course the Prosecution have already said, at the end of the day it doesn't really matter to the Prosecution whether it's Rule 64 or Rule 65, so long as they are in a position to judge that the accused is being held under similar stricture. That poses a third -- another question and another -- I make this as an observation rather than a suggestion because it seems to me that once a person is outside the jurisdiction either of the host country or of the immediate jurisdiction of the UNDF, then the question of good faith really applies as much as anything else. The following of both the letter and the spirit of any conditions which were either imposed by way of a request under Rule 64 or an imposition under Rule 65 are conditions which have to be complied with not so much by the accused but by those who are immediately responsible for his detention and treatment, and the compliance with those rules at the end of the day when someone is away from the immediate control of the Tribunal is one of good faith. So it seems to me that that's the real issue. Is there going to be good faith played by the parties who are in immediate control of the accused? We are not here talking about a simple detention. We are talking about him being in the hands of professional people, and it seems to me that in those circumstances there is abundant reason to suppose that there will be such good faith and the primary concern of those people will be the mental health of this defendant, and as that is going to be the primary concern of the Tribunal, those two concerns are correlated and will be observed, for instance, if he went to Serbia by the Serbian authorities. So it seems to me that if everybody is working towards the same end, then that's as good an indication as we are likely to get that the defendant would, if necessary, be present at any other -- at any future hearing at which his presence was required or indeed at any future trial should that eventuality ever happen. The reality is in this case that if the accused is sent for treatment, he is not going to be arbitrarily released into any other community as long as the question of his being a danger to himself or a danger to the public is still a live issue. It seems to me that we are going perhaps too far down the road into speculation about whether or not at the end of the day the worries of the -- just enunciated by my learned friend are real worries about whether he needs -- we need to worry about the issue of enforced treatment. I think that's -- it's too early to worry about that. The realpolitik of any treatment of any person whether it's mental illness or physical illness is this: Does the person cooperate? That is something which we can only see by testing the system, by putting the accused into a system and seeing whether he does, in fact, take his medication and cooperate. All the indications are that he will, and I say that because he has been given medication in the past. He is being given medication at present, and all the signs are that he is cooperating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put one question to you, Mr. Morrison. You say if the accused is sent for treatment he is not going to be arbitrarily released into any other community as long as the question of his being a danger to himself or a danger to the public is still a live issue. How in your mind could this be effected by provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: By paragraph 65(C): The Trial Chamber may put conditions on the released of the accused as it determines appropriate including the terms of a bail bond - well, that's not realistic in this case - "and the observance of such conditions are necessary to ensure the presence of the accused for trial and the protection of others." It seems that those latter conditions are exactly on point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now the other side of that problem, that if for whatever reasons, let's not forget that the accused is diagnosed as psychotic, if he would not fulfil any of the these conditions, what in your then view should happen? This should be reported to the Chamber by one of the parties, I take it. Then we would hear the parties on that and take a decision that provisional release will be reversed, or what in your mind -- also in view of the time one would need to respond to such uncertain developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost the reality is this, that if he was, for instance, in a Serbian psychiatric hospital, there is going to be no distinction there between Rule 64 and Rule 65 as to the conditions imposed upon him. He -- the conditions can be literally the same conditions, and the effect upon the authorities will be exactly the same. Should the accused fail of his own volition to comply with those conditions, one would expect the responsible authorities to report that with some immediacy to the Tribunal, and the Tribunal can then hold a hearing, first of all to determine -- there seems to be two aspects to it. First of all to determine whether or not that's true, that the accused person has in fact failed to comply with the conditions. If he is found that he has in fact failed to comply with the conditions, there would need to be then the possibility of separate representation from both the OTP and the Defence as to what the consequences of that may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my main question is you say under Rule 64 and 65 you could impose the same conditions. Is it true that under Rule 64 one could impose conditions of detention, which means that there is a situation of detention, whereas in the context of a provisional release, one could impose conditions upon the accused, but would that justify a deprivation of liberty? That's the main issue. I mean, on what basis could the government of state X say, "You should stay within these walls"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: That would have to be a state undertaking by the government. But that depends on the bona fides of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if the government is depriving someone of his liberty, usually you need a basis that should be provided by law. What, in your mind, under these circumstances would be the legal basis for this detention where the Tribunal has provisionally released the accused from detention?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If the provisional release from the custody of the Tribunal was on the basis that he stay and reside in a named mental institution, then it seems to me that that -- that that covers that possibility. If a lawyer was to say differently and to apply to the government for a writ of habeas corpus saying that person is unlawfully detained, then it seems to me that the detaining state could say, "Well, all we are doing is complying in good faith with the conditions imposed upon us by the ICTY," which is all they would do in reality if there was a detention under Rule 64. It seems to me that there is very little practical distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it your interpretation of Rule 65 that apart from voluntary commitments made by a state that also conditions could be imposed upon a state in the framework of conditional release?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I suppose they're imposed upon the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: And you ask for the active cooperation of the state both in Rule 64 and 65 in reality, because without the bona fides and the cooperation of the state neither Rule 64 or 65 would bite. But there is -- an analogy I would think of is in the United Kingdom and I'm sure in America we have, and perhaps in Holland, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're broadening the basis, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: There is a provisional release in the sense that somebody is given bail but there is a curfew. They are given bail but they must stay within the curtilage of their dwelling house between 6.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m. So they are confined within their house. That's very much -- the onus is then upon the accused to maintain that curfew but it is nevertheless a deprivation of liberty, and it seems to me that a provisional release by the Tribunal with a curfew of a 24-hour stay in a mental institution is no different in reality than detention. I'm -- I suppose what I'm trying to seek to try and do is absolve the President from the necessity of dealing with matters which can properly be dealt with by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we must -- let me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- you're finished your observations in respect of this legal issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the distinction between Rule 65 and Rule 64 is concerned, we take in effect the same position that the OTP takes, that as long as the accused person is in a -- a proper institution, receiving appropriate treatment, the exact methodology by which he came to be there is perhaps academic. The effect -- the effectiveness of the treatment really relies upon two things, first of all the competence of the people treating him; and secondly, his degree of cooperation. I think we can assume the competence and cooperation. The competence by virtue of the qualifications of the staff, the cooperation by looking at the history of how he has cooperated up to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question for the Prosecution is the following: What should the prospects of future ability to enter a plea or to stand trial be in order to deprive an accused for a longer period of time from his liberty? You understand what I mean? I mean, actually the completion strategy lasts until 2010. Is it the position of the Prosecution that -- well, every six months we would have to look at the medical condition of someone who is not free to move as one who cooperates in his treatment? What is the position of the Prosecution in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's position is give it six months and see whether the accused responds to treatment, then reassess the matter then. The Prosecutor says it is premature to go down the path of the completion strategy or the transitional arrangement which may occur afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a let's wait and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a let's wait and see situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A let's wait and see situation of course involves detention even if what we see at the end would not justify detention any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We don't know what's going to happen in six months' time, which is why the Prosecutor is loath to express a finalised view on the matter which Your Honour has just raised, and the Prosecutor says it doesn't yet really arise for a determination. Your Honour, might I -- there was something Mr. Morrison said a moment ago that I might be able to assist on -- as of another -- another analogy, a domestic analogy and that is in relation to the Rule 65(C) obligation. The Prosecutor says that the -- I mean the state in the former Yugoslavia obviously has an obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal, and if it were provisional release under 65(C) the obligation is clearly on the state and each state has its own laws on cooperation with the Tribunal. A domestic analogy -- my learned friend Mr. Morrison referred to a curfew. The more appropriate one is the release of a prisoner who is detained to bail or provisional release to undergo drug treatment at a specified location with -- the reality of the release is the person is confined or basically locked into a drug treatment programme which they can't leave and leaving the drug treatment programme which is a secure facility would be a breach of bail resulting in their immediate reincarceration back in the mainstream prison population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Is there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any further issue the parties would like to raise at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. The Prosecutor has asked us to put this matter before the Trial Chamber, and that is the Prosecutor considers this is a matter that the President might look at under Rule 11 bis in the future either before or after the six months that the Trial Chamber has been talking about. That is why the Prosecutor says that some of the issues on the list which Mr. Harhoff circulated for comment may not arise at the moment such as the medical consequences if the accused is permanently incompetent to stand trial, or the criminal legal consequences and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just try to understand you. At this moment, no cases have been transferred to the former Yugoslavia. Has there any?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: None that -- none that we're aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, none. So this would be then the first one. The first one would be of a psychiatric patient to the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro where as far as I'm aware already for quite some time preparations are made in order to prepare for the first case, for example Bosnia where a special court is -- is designed to be created for -- for those purposes. Is that -- I mean, if I look at what it needs to prepare for such a transfer under normal circumstances, not the exceptional circumstances we need here, what makes the Prosecutor or the Prosecution consider this case to be a very problematic case in this respect, I would say, to be the first one to a place where preparations seem not to have been developed in a similar way as in other states of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm certainly not saying this is or will be the first case to be dealt with under Rule 11 bis. The Prosecutor's view is to inform the Trial Chamber that this is a matter which the President may wish to look at in the future as a potential one which falls within the provisions of Rule 11 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. Any further issues to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It really depends upon the competence of the -- it really depends on the competence of the accused. I can't imagine if the accused was judged to be competent to be tried in the sort of time scale that we know that this Tribunal will subsist for that he wouldn't be tried. Likewise, if he were adjudged to be incompetent as far as the tests of this Tribunal are concerned, it seems to be wholly unlikely that he would be adjudged competent to be tried in Serbia or indeed any other jurisdiction. So I think the wait and see provisions apply more to Rule 11 bis than any other part of the discussions we've had so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Finally, Mr. Kovacevic, I'd like to address you, because a lot has been said and that was all about you. It was about your medical condition. It was also about, may I say so, your future in court or in hospital. The Chamber was a bit surprised, as a matter of fact, that you would agree to go back to Belgrade for treatment in view of your -- in view of the previous position you've taken. Could you explain the Court and to what extent or for what reason you changed your mind or you -- that your position is different from what it used to be where you preferred not to -- not to come too close to psychiatrists from Belgrade? Could you explain to the Court what happened that you now instructed counsel to agree with a treatment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain this a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really follow this. What kind of treatment in Belgrade do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have been talking, Mr. Kovacevic, about psychiatric treatment that you would need both --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- both your counsel and the Prosecution agree that you would need such treatment, and one of the issues we have been discussing as well is if you would undergo such treatment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where you would undergo that, and we heard --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from counsel that you would agree with such treatment to be undergone in Belgrade in a psychiatric hospital. We have not yet inquired in any detail --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Whether that would be possible. But previously, you have given this Chamber the impression that you didn't trust very much --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Serbian government or Serbian institutions --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and now, nevertheless, we do understand that you agree with a treatment even if it would be in a Belgrade psychiatric facility. What made you change your mind that you now sufficiently trust the doctors or the authorities in Belgrade to undergo treatment there where you seemed so much to be opposed against it when we saw you one of the previous times?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They tied me to a bed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But now these people have retired. They put you in a barred room, and they tie you to a bed. But now these people have retired. Now other people have come, and they are much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The head of the Military Medical Academy is a person you certainly know. He said that he would help me, that he would help me to get better, and he told me I was welcome and that he would make it possible for me to receive treatment and be cured if possible. And he is ready to take me there. You know, it wouldn't be like that iron door in Scheveningen like here, you know. We're inside for 24 hours in those rooms, you know, and then these doctors come and we work, too. We make vases and bandages and things. I think it's better now. Those people before were dangerous. They would tie people to beds, and then you'd stay in bed all the time tied to the bed. They wouldn't allow you to move about at all. Now he told me that he wouldn't do that kind of thing? He would try to take good care of me. Isn't that what he said. Tanja, isn't that what he said. Tanja, isn't that what Dr. Stankovic said, the bald one. Do you know him? Stankovic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a nice man. Yes, yes, nice man. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you explained to us now that because they are not the same people any more that you have better expectations that you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are not the same. Not the same, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore, you have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other ones worked for state security. They were dangerous. They were not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you expect these new people to assist you in recovering --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two different types of treatment that I'm there for 24 hours round the clock and the other type is that I would go in at a given point in time. I'd have breakfast and then therapy and then group therapy and then psychoanalysis and then I would do what I would be ordered to do and then at 1500 hours they would say you can go home now, come back tomorrow morning at 7.00. Then I'd come back at 7.00. So that's what I do, whatever they ordered me to do. And then they'd say on Sunday you go to a monastery. Then I go to a monastery, I pray to God. I do what they tell me to do. And then they had take us in groups to monasteries and then we'd spend a bit of time in the monastery. That's the kind of regimen that is followed. It's not like those other ones that tie you to a bed. And I don't know why they're tying me here, too. I mean, where would I run away through these halls. Where would I run away? What would I do. I mean, even if I were to run away where I would go? What would I do. I don't know the town, I don't know the language. I have nowhere to escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what if you would have to stay --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what if you would have to stay for the full 24 hours a day in that psychiatric facility because you're now speculating on another type of treatment which would allow you to leave the institution in the late afternoon and return the next morning, but what if you would have to stay there for the full 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already been there for treatment 24 hours a day. That's where they retired me. This service, this security service was bothered by me for some reason. They said I was no longer fit for the military. I don't know what they did to me. I had to take this medication, and then this lady doctor, she kept watching all the time whether I was taking this medicine or not, and then she would order me to take a glass of water and I'd have to drink it. She's like an officer there. She issues orders. What can you do? And she says drink it and of course I drink it. What can I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now since Dr. Stankovic is there, I trust him. I would trust him. As for those who were there until now, I wouldn't trust them. They all belong to the security service. They're all spies, and there is something wrong with them. They work for some intelligence service. And now since Dr. Stankovic is there, Tanja, you're the one who told me this; right? Did you tell me that, Tanja? Tanja? Tanja said to me that Dr. Stankovic said that he sent a message to me saying that he would try to cure me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether he could do something, well -- but you know, that's what the regimen is there. I've been through all of that already. But I mean being tied to a bed with those straps, no, I couldn't take that. I'd have to oppose that. And Dr. Stankovic, General Stankovic says that they would not tie me down any longer, that his men would work with me and that they'd work with me nicely and then I would do as ordered, and if they would tell me at 1500 hours go home, have lunch and come back tomorrow morning at 7.00, I'd do that. And now if this would give any results, I could go back to my family. I have four children. My little son Milos has the measles now. He can't come. I can't see him. And we live a very poor life, but then -- well, I don't know. Well, whatever you say. Whatever you say. It's your decision. There is a saying in Montenegro where I come from that the head is mine, the sword is yours. Now, you decide. I thought that I wasn't sick, but I seem to feel sick now. I will accept what the doctors tell me, but I am afraid that they'll poison me. Vera gives me one set of medicine and then another set and then third medicine. And now this Stankovic, if he were to treat me, I think he would cure me. He talked to me once and this is what he said to Tanja, and that means a great deal to me. Now it's for you to decide. So whatever you decide. I do thank you. May I sit down now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may sit down now if you want to, but I've got one more question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said -- you told us that you at least hope and perhaps even expect that Dr. Stankovic could cure you or at least to improve your situation in such a way that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you are cured or if you your condition improves --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that the Prosecution might insist on you having to stand trial --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- once you are in a better --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. I wanted to come on the 9th, too, but they arrested me. I reported to the assistant Minister, Mihajlovic. I had already volunteered once to come before this Tribunal. Then Minister Mihajlovic said, "Don't go now because you'll harm Admiral Jokic." So they prevented me from doing this and they entered my apartment and they stole my documents and my cassettes and everything. They want to blame everything on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not the one who commanded the army. I was not the one who carried out the mobilisation. It was the generals and admirals who did this. There was 160 captains there and I was one of them. I was a captain at the time. It's not that I had that kind of rank or I had completed that had kind of school. It's not that I led so many people. But even the number of people I did lead was a great burden for me, and so many people getting killed and harmed, that's why I got sick, because I had no way of dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, your last remarks go into the subject of the case against you where I intended only to discuss here the procedural perspectives of this case rather than to go into the subject matter of this case. Was this what you would like to tell the Court at the end of this hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I'm better, I will report myself, and I'll come here and explain who is guilty of all of this. I'll say all of that myself. I'll come myself. You don't have to set any deadlines. Sixty days or six months or 6.000 days, I'm going to say this myself. I'm going to say I'm going to see this gentleman -- I'm sorry I don't know your name -- and I'm going to say what I have to say to him. I'm not afraid of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the people from the family I come from were honourable men. I'm not afraid of anything. Everybody can come here and I can say everything. And now he's -- now he's become forgetful. Now he cannot remember this and he cannot remember that and now a captain is to be blamed for everything, the one whose shoulders were the smallest. I'm speaking from my heart, from my soul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I fully understand that you're speaking from your heart. You again entered into the case itself rather than to speak about the procedure, or perspectives, but your message that you gave is entirely clear. You total the Court that as soon as you have recovered that you'd like to come and be in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This message is perfectly --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Kovacevic. If there is nothing else to be raise at this moment we will adjourn and Chamber will consider how to proceed in the present circumstances. We will give a written decision in respect of this issue. We will adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: ---  Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
